text: William Kentridge, born on 28 April 1955 in Johannesburg to Sydney Kentridge and Felicia Geffen, a Jewish family of lawyers who defended victims of apartheid, is a South African artist renowned for his prints, drawings, and animated films. He began showing artistic promise at age eight, taking charcoal classes, and earned a Bachelor of Arts in Politics and African Studies from the University of the Witwatersrand, followed by a diploma in Fine Arts from the Johannesburg Art Foundation. In the early 1980s, he studied mime and theatre at the L'École Internationale de Théâtre Jacques Lecoq in Paris, where he realized he was not suited for acting and transitioned to becoming an artist. Between 1975 and 1991, he acted and directed with Johannesburg's Junction Avenue Theatre Company and worked on television films as an art director. Kentridge's work is deeply rooted in South Africa's socio-political history, and he views his ethnic Jewish identity as offering a third-party perspective. He practices expressionist art where form and content are interwoven, and his sparse, rough handwriting evokes a sombre, vulnerable atmosphere. His art frequently addresses social injustice, such as in *Casspirs Full of Love*, a print that appears as heads in boxes to outsiders but symbolizes apartheid-era crowd-control vehicles used against lower-class populations. By the mid-1970s, he produced prints and drawings, including the "Pit" series (1979) and "Domestic Scenes" (1980), which established his artistic identity. In 1986, he created charcoal and pastel drawings inspired by Watteau's *The Embarkation for Cythera*, depicting a dystopic urban landscape. In 1996–1997, he produced *Ubu Tells the Truth*, a portfolio based on Alfred Jarry's *Ubu Roi*, relating to South Africa's Truth and Reconciliation Commission. In 2012, he delivered the Norton Lectures at Harvard University, discussing studio practice and a series of large tree drawings made on torn encyclopedia pages. Kentridge's animated films, beginning with *Johannesburg, 2nd Greatest City After Paris* in 1989 and continuing through *Tide Table* (2003) and *Other Faces* (2011), use a unique technique of successive charcoal drawings on the same sheet, with erasures and re-drawings giving each change a quarter to two seconds of screen time, preserving traces of previous images to convey fading memory and time's passage. These films feature characters Soho Eckstein and Felix Teitlebaum, reflecting the emotional and political struggles of pre-democracy South Africa. His work explores themes of time, change, and suppressed history, often through ambiguity, contradiction, and unfinished narratives. In 1988, he co-founded the Free Film-makers Co-Operative in Johannesburg; in 1999, he was appointed a filmmaker by Stereoscope. His political perspective is evident in his opera productions, including *Il ritorno d'Ulisse in patria*, *Die Zauberflöte*, and *The Nose*, and in the collaborative show *Telegrams from the Nose*. In 2015, his staging of Berg's *Lulu* premiered at the Metropolitan Opera, and in 2017, his *Wozzeck* premiered at the Salzburg Festival. In 2023, he won the Laurence Olivier Award for Outstanding Achievement in Opera for *Sybil* at the Barbican Theatre. Kentridge began a series of tapestries in 2001, using shadowy figures from ripped construction paper and nineteenth-century atlas maps, collaborating with the Johannesburg-based Stephens Tapestry Studio to create locally spun mohair tapestries. In 2009, he created the 10m-tall sculpture *Fire Walker* in Johannesburg and *Il cavaliere di Toledo* in Naples; in 2013, he produced *Rebus*, a series of bronze sculptures that form a nude when paired at a certain angle. In 2016, he unveiled *Triumphs and Laments*, a 550m-long mural along the Tiber River in Rome, celebrating the city's founding in 753BC with over 80 figures from mythology to the present, accompanied by live shadow play and music. Kentridge is married to Anne Stanwix and has three children; he is of third-generation South African Lithuanian-Jewish heritage. His films were shown at the 2004 Cannes Film Festival. His works are held in permanent collections at the Honolulu Museum of Art, Kalamazoo Institute of Arts, Museum of Contemporary Art, Chicago, Museum of Modern Art (New York), and Tate Modern (London). An edition of *The Refusal of Time* (2012) was acquired by the Metropolitan Museum of Art and the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art. In 2015, he donated his complete archive of films, videos, and digital works to the George Eastman Museum. His *Five Themes* exhibit was included in the 2009 Time 100 and won First Place in the 2009 AICA Best Monographic Museum Show Nationally category. In 2012, he was invited to deliver the Charles Eliot Norton Lectures at Harvard University and was elected to the American Philosophical Society. In 2017, he founded The Centre For The Less Good Idea in Maboneng, Johannesburg, with Bronwyn Lace, currently led by Neo Muyanga. Kentridge's artworks are among the most valuable in South Africa, with a major charcoal drawing selling for £250,000; a bronze piece reached $1.5 million at Sotheby's New York in 2013, and a record of R6.6 million ($320,000) was set in 2018 at Aspire Art Auctions in Johannesburg. He is represented by Goodman Gallery, Lia Rumma Gallery, and Hauser & Wirth (since 2024), having worked with Goodman Gallery from 1999 to 2024.
